clue.text: Distemper firm's accommodation

parts.note: firm means hard; the 's is a link meaning has
a pad is slang for a flat or place to live

explanation.surface: A firm's lodgings have been painted with distemper.
explanation.walkthrough: Distemper looks like the wall paint, but it is the dog disease.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardpad is a form of canine distemper that hardens the pads of a dog's feet.

clue.text: Hound has almost killed badger

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: almost says the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: slew is the past tense of slay, to kill

explanation.surface: A dog has nearly killed a badger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last letter of SLEW. Hound looks like the dog and badger the animal; both are verbs meaning pester, so badger restates the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To pester or harass someone persistently is to keep after them.

clue.text: Book about earlier mediaeval instrument

indicators.note: earlier says the instrument goes before the abbreviation for about

parts.note: a rebec is a mediaeval bowed stringed instrument
ca, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A book on an old medieval instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Daphne du Maurier's novel of this name is the book.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel by Daphne du Maurier carries this title.

clue.text: Good manners of a couple of girls, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the words are spoken and matched by their sound

parts.note: Polly and Tess are two girls' names

explanation.surface: Two girls are said to be polite.
explanation.definitionFit: This French borrowing means formal courtesy or etiquette.

clue.text: Repeated offence that's penalised in court

definitions.text: Repeated offence that's penalised in court

parts.words: Repeated offence that's penalised in court
parts.note: on a tennis court, two failed serves in a row lose the point

explanation.surface: A second offence is punished by a judge.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis, two consecutive missed serves forfeit the point, a twice-made error on court.

clue.text: Bail's supporter appearing before judge to pay

parts.note: in cricket the bails rest on top of the stumps
to be up before the judge is to be in court

explanation.surface: Someone appearing before a judge on bail must find the money.
explanation.walkthrough: Bail looks legal, as does judge; a bail here is one of the small wooden crosspieces sitting on the cricket stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: To stump up is an informal British idiom for handing over money owed.

clue.text: Clock or watch

definitions.meaning: to clock is slang for to notice or spot

explanation.surface: A clock or a wristwatch.
explanation.definitionFit: Both slangy clocking and watching mean noticing or observing with the eyes.

clue.text: Not expected to be so excessive

parts.note: un- is the prefix meaning not
due means expected, as a train is due

explanation.surface: Something unforeseen proves to be too much.
explanation.definitionFit: Undue means more than is warranted, beyond what is proper.

clue.text: Writes about classical goddess or — gods

indicators.note: about says the writing verb goes round the goddess

parts.note: pens means writes
Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and ruin

explanation.surface: Someone writes about an ancient goddess or the gods.
explanation.definitionFit: The Penates were the Roman household deities guarding the storeroom.

clue.text: Christian's movement

parts.note: Christian is the hero of Bunyan's allegory The Pilgrim's ..., whose journey is his advance

explanation.surface: A Christian religious movement.
explanation.walkthrough: Christian looks like a believer generally; he is Bunyan's pilgrim.
explanation.definitionFit: Forward movement or advance, and the last word of Bunyan's title The Pilgrim's ..., whose hero is Christian.

clue.text: Uses a club, breaking one part of the law, possibly

definitions.text: one part of the law, possibly

indicators.note: breaking suggests the letters of the preceding words are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone wielding a club is breaking the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' rearranges USES A CLUB; 'possibly' warns that a law need not have this part.
explanation.definitionFit: A statute is divided into clauses and their subdivisions, so a subsidiary clause is one portion of it.

clue.text: Colloquial contraction used by the ignorant

definitions.text: Colloquial contraction used by the ignorant

parts.words: Colloquial contraction used by the ignorant
parts.note: a slangy squashing of 'don't know', which is what someone without the answer says

explanation.surface: A slang shortening is favoured by uneducated speakers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a slurred running together of 'don't know', said by someone lacking knowledge.

clue.text: Left one court I entered, in accordance with law

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: I entered says the letter goes into the court abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone who went left into a courtroom insists it was all lawful.
explanation.definitionFit: Licit means lawful or permitted, the opposite of illicit.

clue.text: Elizabeth's favourite cheese

definitions.meaning: Robert Dudley, Earl of ..., was the favourite courtier of Elizabeth I
An English hard cheese named after the county

explanation.surface: The Queen's preferred cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth I's favourite courtier was Robert Dudley, Earl of that title, and the English county also names a red hard cheese.

clue.text: She's left something held by her single lock

parts.note: held by something is being in it
taken as written
single means one, the Roman numeral I
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: A woman with one lock of hair has been bequeathed something.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who receives a bequest is an heiress, one to whom property was left.

clue.text: Swears violently about weak champion in struggle for power.

indicators.note: about says the scrambled letters go round the next pieces
violently suggests the word swears is thrown about into a new order

parts.note: weak means soft
a champion is a hero

explanation.surface: Someone curses violently at a feeble champion during a power struggle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'violently' scrambles the first word and 'about' wraps it round the next pieces; Swears looks like the subject of the sentence but is only fodder. The answer is the 15th-century English civil war.
explanation.definitionFit: The fifteenth-century English dynastic conflict between York and Lancaster was a long fight for the throne.

clue.text: Going to Gibraltar? It's inaccessible

parts.note: Gibraltar is known as the Rock
bound means heading for, as in homeward bound

explanation.surface: A traveller heading for Gibraltar is told it cannot be reached.
explanation.definitionFit: Hemmed in by crags, a place so enclosed cannot be reached easily.

clue.text: Stop working and be a thief

definitions.meaning: to finish work for the day

explanation.surface: Someone stops working and turns to theft.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to finish work for the day and, slangily, to steal.

clue.text: Upstarts more generally understood in Paris?

definitions.text: Upstarts more generally understood in Paris?

parts.words: Upstarts more generally understood in Paris?
parts.note: the French term for social climbers who have recently made money, a phrase whose meaning is clearer in its home city

explanation.surface: Social climbers are better understood by the French.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase for the newly wealthy describes vulgar upstarts who have made money but lack breeding.

clue.text: Normally acceptable within Britain in terms of special relationship?

indicators.note: within says the letter goes inside the phrase for Britain

parts.words: Britain in terms of special relationship
parts.note: in the special relationship Britain is the US's partner, a US ally
U means socially acceptable, upper-class usage

explanation.surface: Something is normally acceptable in Britain because of its special relationship with America.
explanation.walkthrough: The special relationship is the name for close UK–US ties.
explanation.definitionFit: Normally and as a rule both mean in most cases.

clue.text: Somehow learnt about hard grip

indicators.note: about says the scrambled letters go round the next piece
somehow suggests the letters of learnt are put in some new order

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone learnt something about a firm hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' scrambles the first word and 'about' wraps the result round the letter for hard; grip is a verb here, to captivate.
explanation.definitionFit: To grip an audience is to hold it spellbound, to captivate it.

clue.text: Dog some breeders had owned

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Breeders once owned a particular dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Dog looks like the animal; here it is the verb to follow closely.
explanation.definitionFit: To dog someone is to follow them closely, to tail them.

clue.text: Acted and put old order out, in this

definitions.text: Acted and put old order out, in this

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are disordered and laid out afresh

explanation.surface: In this event, people acted to remove the established regime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges ACTED, PUT and O; the whole clue also describes the event.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden seizure of government overthrows the established regime, which is what the whole clue describes.

clue.text: Discourage person wanting to lose weight? Not I!

indicators.note: Not I says the letter I is taken away from the slimmer

parts.note: a dieter wants to slim

explanation.surface: A slimmer is put off, but the speaker denies being one.
explanation.definitionFit: To deter is to put off or dissuade.

clue.text: Make a mistake dividing the two by a hundred

indicators.note: dividing says one piece splits the other by sitting in its middle

parts.note: the two together means both
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Someone errs when splitting a pair by a hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: To bungle or mess up a job is to spoil it through error.

clue.text: Small bird's cry of pain, having suffered

parts.note: ow is an exclamation of pain
suffered in its old sense of allowed means let

explanation.surface: A little bird cries out after being hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffered' has its biblical sense of permitted, as in 'suffer the little children'.
explanation.definitionFit: A young owl is a small bird.

clue.text: Like some boards, having fluctuating fortune

definitions.meaning: draughts boards are marked in alternating squares
a career with ups and downs, as in a varied past

explanation.surface: Some boards share the mixed luck of a life.
explanation.definitionFit: A draughts board has a checked pattern, and a varied history full of ups and downs is described the same way.

clue.text: Suffer arrest

explanation.surface: Someone suffers being arrested.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang verb means both to catch a criminal and, as cop it, to be punished.

clue.text: Plant where carriages are assembled

parts.note: a fly is a light horse-drawn hired carriage
a trap is a light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage

explanation.surface: A factory floor where carriages are put together.
explanation.walkthrough: Plant suggests a factory; it is the carnivorous vegetable, and FLY and TRAP are both old horse-drawn vehicles.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venus variety is a carnivorous botanical species that snaps shut on insects.

clue.text: Pessimistic view of life set out in old saws

indicators.note: set out suggests the words are rearranged into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A gloomy outlook expressed in proverbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set out' rearranges OLD SAWS. The answer is British slang for the rule that whatever can go wrong will.
explanation.definitionFit: This British maxim holds that anything that can go wrong will, a gloomy outlook.
